1.note: Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

2.note: The word **you** is singular here because Moses is being addressed individually. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

2.q: עֲשֵׂ֣ה לְ⁠ךָ֗ שְׁתֵּי֙ חֲצֽוֹצְרֹ֣ת כֶּ֔סֶף & תַּעֲשֶׂ֣ה
2.note: By **Make for you**, Yahweh means that Moses should have someone make the trumpets for him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Let two trumpets of silver be made for you. Let them be made of]

A **hammered work** is a kind of metalworking technique where a flat sheet of metal is shaped by striking it repeatedly. If your readers would not be familiar with what a hammered work is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. See how you translated this phrase in 8:4. Alternate translation: [from a sheet of silver that was hammered into shape]

The implication is that someone other than Moses would need to blow the trumpets. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and you shall have someone blow them]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **assembly** and **departure**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to signal the congregation to assemble and to signal the camps to depart]

Here, **camps** represents the groups of people living in the camps. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people in the camps]

3.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the priests, as 10:8 clarifies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the priests shall blow]

The implication is that Moses was to have both trumpets sounded to summon the entire congregation, in contrast with 10:4, where only one trumpet was to be sounded to summon just the leaders. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the two trumpets]
The word **you** is singular here because Moses is the one being addressed. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

4.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [a single trumpet]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the leaders of Israel were actually **heads** of groups of people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chiefs over the divisions within Israel]
The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is speaking only to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

5.note: The word **you** is plural here because God is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **you shall blow**, Yahweh means that the priests shall blow the trumpets. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And you shall have the priests blow]

A **alarm** is a kind of signal made by blowing the trumpet in a special way. If your readers would not be familiar with what an alarm is, you could use a more general term or explain it in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a signal] or [a loud blast]

Here, **camps** represents the people living in the camps. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people in the camps]

The implication is that these camps were pitched to the east of the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the east of the tent of meeting]

6.note: The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

By **you shall blow**, Yahweh means that the priests shall blow the trumpets, as stated in 10:8. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this phrase in 10:5. Alternate translation: [and you shall have the priests blow]

The term **alarm** refers to a kind of trumpet signal. If your readers would not be familiar with what an alarm is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term like “signal” or “loud blast.” See how you translated the word **alarm** in 10:5. Alternate translation: [a second signal … a signal] or [a second loud blast … a loud blast]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **a second alarm**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [alarm two]
See how you translated **camps** in 10:5. Alternate translation: [and the people in the camps]

The implication is that these were the camps located to the south of the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 10:5. Alternate translation: [to the south of the tent of meeting]

The pronoun **they** refers to the priests. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated “and they shall blow them” in 10:3. Alternate translation: [And the priests shall blow an alarm for the setting out of the camps]

The implication is that the same trumpet signal used for the eastern and southern camps was also to be used when the western and northern camps set out. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They shall blow alarms for the setting out of each other camp in the same way]

7.note: This is poetic language where the verb “assemble” and its object “assembly” come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And when assembling the people]
The word **you** is plural here because God is speaking to all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The implication is that it is the priests who blow the trumpets, as stated explicitly in 10:8. You could make this explicit by saying who does the blowing. See how you translated “you shall blow” in 10:5. Alternate translation: [you shall have the priests blow but you shall not have them blow]

8.note: Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the priests were actually **sons of Aaron**. This refers to the descendants of Aaron who served as priests. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the men descended from Aaron]
The pronoun **they** refers to the trumpets. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the trumpets shall be]
The word **you** is plural here because it refers to the Israelites. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **statute** that applies for **eternity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for a statute that applies for eternity]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for an eternal statute]

9.note: The word **you** here and in the rest of this verse is plural because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [those who oppose you]
See how you translated this phrase in 10:5.

The expressions **shall be remembered** and **shall be saved** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the actions, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh your God shall remember you, and he shall save you]

The word translated as **and** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and in response you shall be remembered]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh your God]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh your God**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [to my face, who am Yahweh your God]

10.q: וּ⁠בְ⁠י֨וֹם שִׂמְחַתְ⁠כֶ֥ם וּֽ⁠בְ⁠מוֹעֲדֵי⁠כֶם֮ וּ⁠בְ⁠רָאשֵׁ֣י חָדְשֵׁי⁠כֶם֒ וּ⁠תְקַעְתֶּ֣ם בַּ⁠חֲצֹֽצְרֹ֗ת עַ֚ל עֹלֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠עַ֖ל זִבְחֵ֣י שַׁלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם וְ⁠הָי֨וּ לָ⁠כֶ֤ם לְ⁠זִכָּרוֹן֙ לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י אֱלֹֽהֵי⁠כֶ֔ם אֲנִ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵי⁠כֶֽם
10.note: The word **you** is plural here and in the rest of the verse because Yahweh is addressing all the Israelites along with Moses. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, the word **and** in the phrase **and at your appointed times** could mean that: (1) **your appointed times** and **the heads of your months** are examples of **the day of your**. Alternate translation: [And on the day of your joy, that is, at your appointed times and at the heads of your months] (2) **your appointed times** and **the heads of your months** are in addition to **the day of your joy**. Alternate translation: [And on the day of your joy and also at your appointed times and at the heads of your months]
Here, **day** represents a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And at the time of your joy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And on the day when you are joyful]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **day**. He means days in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And on the days]

By **appointed times**, Yahweh means the special festivals that God commanded the Israelites to celebrate each year. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at your yearly festivals]

Here, **heads of your months** refers to the beginning of each month as if each month were a person or animal and its first day were its head. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and during the festivals at the beginning of each month]

The implication is that the priests, not the general population, were to blow the trumpets. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then you shall have the priests blow]

Yahweh is using **upon your burnt offerings and upon the sacrifices of your peace offerings** as a common expression of this culture to mean “when you offer your burnt offerings and when you offer the sacrifices of your peace offerings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when you offer your burnt offerings and when you offer the sacrifices of your peace offerings]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **sacrifices** that are part of **peace offerings**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and upon the animal sacrifices that are part of your peace offerings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **memorial**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they will cause you to be remembered]
Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your God]
Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **your God**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, your God]

11.note: The phrase **And it happened** introduces a new event in the story. This is a common way in biblical Hebrew to signal the beginning of a new section. If your language has a natural way to mark the start of a new event, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [Then] or [After this]

This event took place after the events narrated in Numbers 1–6, which took place after the events in Numbers 7–9. If it is helpful in your language, you might want to make it clear that the account that starts in this verse happened after the events in chapters 1–6. Alternate translation: [after the census, in the second year, in the second month, on 20 in the month]

If your language would not represent numbers in forms such as **in the second year** and **in the second month**, you could represent these numbers in forms that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in year two, in month two]

The implication is that this was two years after the Israelites had left Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the second year after the Israelites left Egypt]

The **second month** of the Hebrew calendar includes April and May on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew day and month into an approximate date on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the date will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the number of the day and the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [on day 20]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **on 20**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [on the twentieth]

The expression **was taken up** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh took the cloud up]

The implication is that the tent housed the stone tablets on which Yahweh had written the Ten Commandments, which were called “the Testimony.” The ark containing these tablets was kept in the Most Holy Place in this tent. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated this phrase in 1:50. Alternate translation: [the tent holding the ark containing the Ten Commandments]

12.note: Here, the word **departures** could refer to: (1) the way each group of three tribes left its campsite. This is probably what the word means in 10:28. Alternate translation: [according to their order of departure] (2) multiple times in a row when the Israelites left their campsite. This is what the word means in [33:1–2](ta:33). Alternate translation: [with many campsites] or [on their many journeys]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **departures**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to how they departed]

The author is speaking of the **cloud** as if it were a living thing that could dwell in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 9:17. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh had the cloud stop and stay]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **wilderness** that is near **Paran**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the wilderness that was near Paran]

13.note: The phrase **in the first** is a common expression of this culture to mean “for the first time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the first time]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **in the first**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [for time one]
See how you translated this phrase in 9:23. Alternate translation: [as Yahweh commanded them under the control of Moses]

14.note: The author is speaking of **the banner** as if it were a living thing that could set out on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And those who camped at the banner of the camp of the sons of Judah set out]

A **banner** is a kind of flag that represents a group of people. If your readers would not be familiar with what a banner is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. See how you translated **banner** in 1:52. Alternate translation: [the flag of]

The implication is that this group, who followed the tribal flag of Judah, included the troops not only from Judah but also from the tribes of Issachar and Zebulun, as shown in 10:15–16. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the camp of the sons of Judah, which included the sons of Issachar and Zeubulun,]

The author is using **in the first** as a common expression of his culture to mean “as the first to leave” or “in the first position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as the first to leave]

Here and throughout the chapter, the phrase **according to their armies** implies that the tribes were organized like armies, with leaders and orderly groups. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the chapter introduction for more information. Alternate translation: [according to their military divisions]
The pronoun **his** refers to Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and over Judah’s army]
For these and the other names in the list in 10:14–27, translate them as you did in chapter 1. See the chapter introduction for more information.

17.note: The expression **was taken down** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Gershonites and the Merarites. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari took down the Dwelling]
See how you translated these men’s names in Numbers 3:17.

The implication is that these men were assigned this task as their specific responsibility. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [whose job it was to carry the Dwelling]

18.note: The author is speaking of **the banner** as if it were a living thing that could move forward. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in 10:14. Alternate translation: [And those who camped at the banner of the camp of Reuben set out]
The pronoun **his** refers to Reuben. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 10:14. Alternate translation: [and over Reuben’s camp]

The implication is that the camp of Reuben included the tribes of Simeon and Gad, who followed Reuben’s leadership and camped near his tribal flag. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the camp of Reuben, which included the sons of Simeon and Gad]

21.note: This refers to the descendants of Kohath. See how you translated this in Numbers 3:27.

The implication is that this group of people had the special duty of carrying the holy place. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in 10:17. Alternate translation: [whose job it was to carry the holy place]

Here, **the holy place** represents the sacred objects that were inside the holy place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. See how you translated the similar phrase in 4:15. Alternate translation: [the things that belong in the holy place]

The pronoun **they** refers to the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari who were mentioned in 2:17. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari raised up]

The author is using **until their coming** as a common expression of his culture to mean “before they arrived.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before they came]

22.q: וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֛גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה בְנֵֽי־אֶפְרַ֖יִם לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ אֱלִישָׁמָ֖ע בֶּן־עַמִּיהֽוּד
22.note: This verse is identical in structure with 10:19 except that this verse includes **the sons of** in front of **Ephraim**. Translate this verse as you translated 10:19, changing only the names as well as **the sons of**, if necessary. The tribes associated with this camp were Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin.

25.q: וְ⁠נָסַ֗ע דֶּ֚גֶל מַחֲנֵ֣ה בְנֵי־דָ֔ן מְאַסֵּ֥ף לְ⁠כָל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֹ֖ת לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠עַל־צְבָא֔⁠וֹ אֲחִיעֶ֖זֶר בֶּן־עַמִּישַׁדָּֽי
25.note: This verse is identical in structure with 10:14 except that it uses the phrase **the one gathering for all the camps** instead of **in the first**. For the phrase **the one gathering for all the camps**, see the note below. Except for that, translate this verse as you translated 10:14. The tribes associated with this camp were Dan, Asher, and Naphtali.

The author is using **the one gathering for all the camps** as a common expression of this culture to mean “the rearguard” or “the one walking at the rear of the group.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one walking at the rear of the group]

28.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **departures**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [This was how the sons of Israel departed]

Here, the word **departures** could refer to: (1) the way each group of three tribes left its campsite. This is probably what the word means in 10:12. Alternate translation: [This was the order of departure of] (2) multiple times in a row when the Israelites left their campsite. This is what the word means in [33:1–2](ta:33). Alternate translation: [These were the many journeys of]

The author assumes that readers will know that he is summarizing what has already been said about how the Israelites arranged themselves for travel. This statement in verse 28 follows the detailed description of the marching order that began in 10:12. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [That is how they set out]

29.note: Here and in 10:31–32, when Moses says **we** and **us**, he is including himself and the Israelites but not Hobab, to whom he is speaking, so use the exclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

It is not totally clear which of these men was Moses’ **father-in-law**. See the chapter introduction for more information. Moses’ **father-in-law** could be: (1) Hobab. Alternate translation: [to the father-in-law of Moses, Hobab the son of Reuel the Midianite] (2) Reuel. Alternate translation: [to Hobab, the son of the father-in-law of Moses, Reuel the Midianite]
The phrase **the Midianite** could go with: (1) Hobab. Alternate translation: [to Hobab the Midianite, the son of Reuel] (2) Reuel. Alternate translation: [to Hobab, the son of Reuel the Midianite]
The words **Hobab** and **Reuel** are the names of men.

29.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ אֶתֵּ֣ן לָ⁠כֶ֑ם
29.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh said that he would give to us]

29.q: לְכָ֤⁠ה אִתָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ וְ⁠הֵטַ֣בְנוּ לָ֔⁠ךְ כִּֽי־יְהוָ֥ה דִּבֶּר־ט֖וֹב עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
29.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has spoken good upon Israel. So, go with us, and we will do good to you]
In a context such as this, your language might say “Come” instead of **Go**. Alternate translation: [Come with us]

Moses is using **has spoken good upon Israel** as a common expression of his culture to mean “has promised to do good things for Israel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has said that good things will happen to Israel]

Moses is speaking of himself and his fellow Israelites in the third person as **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this form in the first person. Alternate translation: [upon us Israelites]

30.q: לֹ֣א אֵלֵ֑ךְ כִּ֧י אִם־אֶל־אַרְצִ֛⁠י וְ⁠אֶל־מוֹלַדְתִּ֖⁠י אֵלֵֽךְ
30.note: If it would appear in your language that Hobab was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I will not go with you. Rather, I will go to my land and to my relatives.]

The phrase **land and relatives** expresses a single idea. The word **relatives** tells more about **land**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [to my land where my relatives are]

31.note: Here and in 10:32, the words **us** and **our** include Moses and the Israelites but not Hobab, to whom Moses is speaking, so use the exclusive form of these words if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [myself and all the Israelites … our camping … for myself and all the Israelites]

Moses is using **For upon this** as a common expression of his culture to mean “Here is why I ask.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Here is why I ask: you know]
Here, **camping** represents places of encampment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [where we can camp]

Moses is using the expression **for us for eyes** as a common expression of his culture to mean “a guide for us.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a guide for us]

32.note: Moses is describing a possible condition in which **it will happen that that good that Yahweh shall do good with us** will take place only if **you go with us** occurs first. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [if you go with us, then it will happen]

32.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֣ה ׀ הַ⁠טּ֣וֹב הַ⁠ה֗וּא אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵיטִ֧יב יְהוָ֛ה עִמָּ֖⁠נוּ וְ⁠הֵטַ֥בְנוּ לָֽ⁠ךְ
32.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **that good that Yahweh shall do good with us** with the information about **we shall do good to you**. Alternate translation: [that we shall do the same good to you that Yahweh shall do with us]

The author does not explicitly indicate whether Hobab went with the Israelites. The narrative may imply that he did. However, because the author does not include Hobab’s response, it is recommended that you do not make his response explicit in your translation.

33.q: וַ⁠יִּסְעוּ֙ מֵ⁠הַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה דֶּ֖רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֑ים
33.note: The term **appointed** is a formal way of saying “arranged for” or “selected for.” If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this idea in a less formal way, such as “he chose” or “he picked.” Alternate translation: [And when they set out from the mountain of Yahweh, they traveled a way of three days]

The implication is that Mount Sinai was the mountain where Yahweh had revealed himself to the Israelites and given them his law. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from Sinai, the mountain of Yahweh]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain** that is characterized by being the place where Yahweh had revealed himself to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the mountain where Yahweh had spoken to them]

33.q: דֶּ֖רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֑ים & דֶּ֚רֶךְ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֔ים
33.note: The phrase **a way of three days** was a common expression of his culture to mean “a three-day journey” or “a distance that would take three days to travel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and walked for three days … for those three days]

The author is speaking of **the box of the covenant of Yahweh** as if it were a living thing that could travel on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the men who carried the box of the covenant of Yahweh were setting out]

Here, **to their face** represents being in front of the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ahead of them]
Here, **rest** represents a place to camp. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a place to rest]

34.q: וַ⁠עֲנַ֧ן יְהוָ֛ה עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֖ם יוֹמָ֑ם בְּ⁠נָסְעָ֖⁠ם מִן־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה
34.note: By **the cloud of Yahweh was over them**, the author means this happened regularly whenever they traveled. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the cloud of Yahweh would be over them by day each time they set out from the camp]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **cloud** that was controlled by **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the cloud that Yahweh controlled]

35.note: The author is speaking of **the box** as if it were a living thing that could set out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when the people who carried the box set out]

The word translated as **Rise up** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you to rise up]

Here, Moses is speaking of the command **Rise up** as if Yahweh were a person who could physically stand up and begin to act. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Begin to act]

The phrases **your enemies will scatter** and **the ones hating you will flee** are results that will follow when Moses says “Rise up, Yahweh.” If it would be clearer in your language, you could use words that show that these are results that will happen when Yahweh acts. Alternate translation: [and in response your enemies will scatter, and in response the ones having you will flee]

Here, **from your face** represents being in the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before you]

36.note: The author is speaking of the box as if it were a living thing that could rest. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when the men carrying it rested]

The implication is that **it** refers to the sacred chest or ark of the covenant that was mentioned in 10:35. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And when it stopped and stayed in one place]

The author is using the present tense in **says** to refer to a repeated past action. If it would not be natural to do that in your language, you could use the past tense in your translation. Alternate translation: [he would say]

This clause could mean that: (1) Moses is asking Yahweh to **Return** to the Israelites after arising (10:35). Alternate translation: [Return, Yahweh, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel] (2) Moses is describing Yahweh as the leader of the Israelites. Alternate translation: [Return, Yahweh who is over the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel]

The word translated as **Return** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [I ask you to return]

Here, Moses is speaking as if Yahweh were actually going to **Return** to a physical location with Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Be with us]

The expression **ten thousands** stands approximately for a very large number. Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [the enormous number of]

Here, Moses is speaking as if the tribes of Israel were **thousands** of military divisions. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the military divisions of]
